relevance_reason: Reports a family with a TGFB3 missense mutation and a marfanoid/LDS-overlapping phenotype (Rienhoff syndrome), which is the subject of LDS5.

findings.statement: Kuechler et al. (2015) described a family in which a father and his 2 children had features overlapping Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes, including tall stature, arachnodactyly, hyperextensible joints, hypertelorism, and bifid uvula. None had cardiac involvement, aortic dilation, or eye involvement.
quotes: The two affected children and their affected father had tall stature, arachnodactyly, hyperextensible joints, hypertelorism, bifid uvula, but no cardiac involvement, aortic dilation or eye involvement.

findings.statement: In 3 affected members of a family with a disorder overlapping Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes, Kuechler et al. (2015) identified a heterozygous c.898C>G mutation in the TGFB3 gene, predicting an arg300-to-gly (R300G) substitution. The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing in 2 affected individuals and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregating with the phenotype. The authors noted that a different mutation at the same codon (R300Q) had previously been reported in a child with overgrowth, and that Arg300 mutations presumably increase TGF-beta signaling.
quotes: We detected a novel heterozygous mutation in TGFB3, c.898C>G, predicting the missense substitution p.Arg300Gly. Sanger sequencing confirmed the mutation and its segregation with the phenotype.
We performed whole exome sequencing in two of three affected individuals from a family with phenotypic features overlapping MFS and LDS.

findings.statement: Kuechler et al. (2015) noted that a heterozygous loss-of-function TGFB3 mutation (C409Y) had been reported in an individual with growth retardation, whereas codon Arg300 mutations, presumably leading to increased TGF-beta signaling, were associated with tall stature/overgrowth, suggesting that short or tall stature in patients with TGFB3 mutations may result from opposing effects on TGF-beta signaling.
quotes: The mutations at codon Arg300 presumably lead to increased TGF-beta signalling, suggesting that the short or tall stature seen in patients with TGFB3 mutations may result from opposing effects of mutations on TGF-beta signalling.

relevance_reason: Reports 43 patients from 11 families with TGFB3 mutations causing syndromic aortic aneurysms and dissections (LDS5), with linkage, mutation identification, clinical delineation and aortic tissue studies.

findings.statement: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) studied a large Dutch family (family 1) with an autosomal dominant disorder whose features overlapped with Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes. Seven members aged 40 to 68 years had aneurysms and dissections, mainly of the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta. Three died of aortic dissection and rupture, and 4 had mitral valve abnormalities ranging from mild prolapse to severe regurgitation. Other features were subtle craniofacial changes (long face, high-arched palate, retrognathia), pectus deformity, scoliosis, velvety skin, varices, hiatal hernia, and autoimmune features including HLA-B27-positive spondyloarthritis, Graves disease, and celiac disease.
quotes: We studied a large Dutch family (family 1) with clinical features overlapping with MFS and LDS consistent with an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Seven family members, between 40 and 68 years of age, presented with aneurysms and dissections, mainly involving the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta

In addition, 4 members had mitral valve abnormalities, ranging from mild prolapse to severe regurgitation requiring surgical intervention. Craniofacial abnormalities were rather subtle, including a long face, high-arched palate, and retrognathia (Figure 2).

Other recurrent findings included velvety skin, varices, and hiatal hernia. Several family members presented with autoimmune features including (HLA-B27 positive) spondyloarthritis, Graves' disease, and celiac disease.

phenotypes.text: descending thoracic and abdominal aortic aneurysm and dissection

findings.statement: In the Dutch family 1, in which all known TAAD genes had been excluded by sequencing, Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) carried out SNP-based linkage analysis in 6 patients. All affected patients shared 2 large genomic regions on chromosomes 14 and 15, and the TGFB3 gene on 14q24 was the leading candidate in these regions.
quotes: Linkage analysis using SNP genotypes from 6 patients of the family identified 2 large genomic regions on chromosomes 14 and 15 shared by all affected patients (Online Figure 1).
Detailed inspection of the genes in the regions identified several candidates, most prominently the TGFB3 gene on 14q24.

findings.statement: In affected members of the Dutch family 1, Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) found a heterozygous TGFB3 splice donor variant in intron 4 (c.754+2T>C). It was absent from variant databases and segregated with the phenotype. Analysis of cDNA from 2 patients showed skipping of exon 4, giving an in-frame deletion of 108 nucleotides and a predicted loss of 36 amino acids (p.Glu216_Lys251del). The variant was also present in a 17-year-old without documented cardiovascular features who had mild systemic findings.
quotes: Subsequent Sanger sequencing of all 7 exons and intron boundaries identified a heterozygous intronic variant affecting the highly conserved (PhastCons: 1, PhyloP: 4.97) canonical donor splice site of exon 4 (c.754+2T>C), which is absent from variant databases

Sequencing of the cDNA for 2 patients (1-II:12 and III:11) confirmed skipping of exon 4, leading to an in-frame deletion of 108 nucleotides (Online Figure 2). At the protein level, a deletion of 36 amino acids is expected (p.Glu216_Lys251del).
This TGFB3 mutation (c.754+2T>C) segregated with the clinical phenotype and was also present in 1 young individual (1-IV:1, 17 years old) without documented cardiovascular features

variants.consequence: splice site; exon 4 skipping, in-frame deletion

findings.statement: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) screened 470 additional probands with syndromic or nonsyndromic TAAD for TGFB3 mutations (350 by Sanger sequencing, 120 by exome sequencing). They found heterozygous TGFB3 mutations in 10 more probands: 4 different missense mutations, 1 nonsense mutation, and 2 single-base deletions causing frameshifts. None of the mutations was found in controls in EVS, 1000 Genomes, or Genome of the Netherlands.
quotes: This revealed additional heterozygous TGFB3 mutations in 10 other probands (7 from Sanger sequencing and 3 from the exome sequencing cohort): 4 different missense mutations, p.Asp263His (family 3), p.Arg300Trp (families 2, 4, 5, 11), p.Ile322Thr (family 10), p.Leu401Pro (family 8); 1 nonsense mutation, p.Tyr365* (family 6)

The causal nature of the TGFB3 mutations was further supported by de novo occurrence (family 6) (Figure 1) and absence from controls (all mutations) in EVS, 1000Genomes, and the Genome of the Netherlands.

findings.statement: In family 3, Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) identified a heterozygous TGFB3 missense mutation, p.Asp263His, in exon 5. It changes a highly conserved residue of the latency-associated peptide (LAP) domain and disrupts the RGD motif needed for integrin binding. In a homology model, Asp263 lies in a surface loop that is accessible to integrins. Aortic tissue from a patient carrying this mutation showed elastic fiber fragmentation and paradoxically increased TGF-beta signaling.
quotes: The p.Asp263His alteration disrupts the Arg-Gly-Asp (RGD) motif, which is essential for binding to the αvß3, αvß6, αvß1, and αvß5 integrins,,.
Asp263 is located in a surface loop where it is accessible for integrins (Figure 4).

findings.statement: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) found a heterozygous TGFB3 missense mutation, p.Arg300Trp, in 4 families (2, 4, 5, and 11). It affects the last amino acid of the LAP domain and disrupts the last residue of the RKKR furin cleavage recognition motif. Homology modeling predicted that ionic interactions would be lost and steric rearrangements induced. Mutations at Arg300 were associated with cleft palate and/or bifid uvula.
quotes: The second missense mutation in exon 5, p.Arg300Trp, affects the last amino acid of the LAP domain, disrupting the last residue of the RKKR minimal recognition motif of the furin or related protease cleavage site (37).

Besides participating in the cleavage site, Arg300 is involved in several ionic interactions that will be lost with the substitution to tryptophan, and this bulky residue will likely induce steric rearrangements.

findings.statement: In family 10, Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) identified a heterozygous TGFB3 missense mutation, p.Ile322Thr, at a highly conserved residue in the active cytokine region. In a homology model, the change was predicted to alter the position of Arg325, a residue important for binding to TGFBR2, and to disrupt hydrophobic contacts with the LAP domain.
quotes: The 2 other missense mutations, p.Ile322Thr and p.Leu401Pro, affect highly conserved amino acids located in the region of the active cytokine.
Ile322Thr is predicted to alter the positioning of Arg325, an important amino acid residue for binding with TGFBR2.

findings.statement: In family 8, Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) identified a heterozygous TGFB3 missense mutation, p.Leu401Pro, at a highly conserved residue in the active cytokine region. The substitution was predicted to change hydrophobic interactions with residues of both the LAP and TGFB3 domains.
quotes: Substitution from Leu401 to proline is predicted to change the hydrophobic interactions with residues of both the LAP and TGFB3 domain.

findings.statement: In the proband of family 6, Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) identified a de novo heterozygous TGFB3 nonsense mutation, p.Tyr365*. The proband also carried a SMAD3 variant of unknown significance (p.Ala250Thr), inherited from a mother who had variable connective tissue findings and mild cardiovascular involvement. The authors considered the contribution of the SMAD3 variant unclear.
quotes: Although p.Tyr365* in family 6 occurred de novo, we previously identified a SMAD3 variant (p.Ala250Thr) of unknown significance in the proband.

This SMAD3 variant was also present in the proband’s mother, who presented with variable connective tissue findings and mild cardiovascular involvement, making its precise contribution to pathogenesis unclear.

findings.statement: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) identified 2 heterozygous single-base deletions in TGFB3 that cause frameshifts and premature stop codons: p.Leu386Argfs*21 in family 7 and p.Asn235Metfs*11 in family 9. The authors predicted that these lead to nonsense-mediated decay or truncated proteins that probably lose cytokine activity.
quotes: 2 single-base deletions leading to a frameshift and premature stop codon, p.Leu386Argfs*21 (family 7) and p.Asn235Metfs*11 (family 9) (Figure 3).

The 3 other mutations create premature stop codons, either in the LAP domain or in the active TGFB3 (cytokine) domain, leading to nonsense-mediated decay or truncated proteins, which probably lose their cytokine activity.

findings.statement: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) summarized 43 patients (23 male, 20 female) from 11 families with TGFB3 mutations. Features overlapped with Loeys-Dietz syndrome. Findings included type A dissection (4 patients; median age 51 years) and type B dissection (6 patients; median age 44.5 years), aortic aneurysm, mitral valve disease, septal defects, hypertelorism, bifid uvula, cleft palate, cervical spine instability, clubfoot, tall stature, arachnodactyly, pectus deformity, kyphoscoliosis, joint hypermobility, and hernia. They observed no early dissection, no dissection at small aortic size, no striking arterial tortuosity, and no ectopia lentis. Clinical variability was striking both within and between families.
quotes: Vascular involvement ranges from no cardiovascular abnormalities at age 64 (3-II:2) to type A (median age of 51 years, range 40 to 80 years) or type B aortic dissection (median age of 44.5 years, range 30 to 57), abdominal aortic dissection and death as a result of cerebral aneurysm dissection at age 55 (2-II:1) (Table 1).
Typical LDS findings such as hypertelorism, bifid uvula and cleft palate, cervical spine instability, and club foot deformity are commonly observed
No evidence for ectopia lentis was found in the medical records. Early-onset osteoarthritis was only reported in 2 individuals (10-II:1 and 11-II:1).

findings.statement: In the dissected aortic wall of a patient with the p.Asp263His mutation, Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) found elastic fiber fragmentation with increased collagen and proteoglycan deposition. Immunohistochemistry showed paradoxically enhanced TGF-beta signaling, with increased pSMAD2 (canonical) and pERK (noncanonical), as well as elevated TGFB1 mRNA, similar to findings in TGFB2-deficient aortas. Pathology reports from 2 family 1 patients also described extensive elastic fiber fragmentation and aortic medial degeneration.
quotes: Microscopic examination of the dissected aortic wall, obtained at the time of surgery (3-III:1), showed elastic fiber fragmentation with higher collagen and proteoglycan deposition (Figures 5A to 5C).

we observed evidence of paradoxically enhanced TGF-β signaling in the aortic wall of a TGFB3 mutant patient, as shown by increased pSMAD2 (canonical TGF-β signaling), pERK (noncanonical TGF-β signaling), and elevated TGFB1 messenger RNA (Figures 5D to 5F).

phenotypes.text: elastic fiber fragmentation of aortic media

findings.statement: Because they found 3 truncating mutations and an in-frame splice site mutation, Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) hypothesized that TGFB3 mutations cause loss of function. They also proposed that the young age of previously reported patients (8 and 10.5 years) might explain why those patients lacked obvious cardiovascular disease.
quotes: Because we observed 3 truncating mutations and an in-frame splice site mutation, we hypothesize that the TGFB3 mutations lead to loss of function (LOF) of TGFB3.
The relatively young age of previously reported patients with TGFB3 mutations (8 [16] and 10.5 years of age [17]) might explain the lack of obvious cardiovascular disease.

findings.statement: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) noted that TGFB3 mutations appeared to have opposing effects on height. One patient with p.Asp263His had short stature and received growth hormone, whereas several others had tall stature. Mutations affecting Arg300 were associated with cleft palate and/or bifid uvula.
quotes: TGFB3 mutations also appear to have opposing effects on height, as 1 patient in this study (3-III:1, p.Asp263His) has short stature and received growth hormone therapy during puberty
TGFB3 mutations affecting residue Arg300 are associated with cleft palate and/or bifid uvula in our patients (Online Tables 3, 4, and 6) and in the patient reported by Matyas et al. (17).

findings.statement: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) recommended yearly echocardiographic evaluation of the aortic root in all TGFB3 mutation carriers, plus at least 1 baseline imaging study of the complete aorta and its side branches. They added that imaging of the brain vessels might be indicated.
quotes: We recommend yearly echocardiographic evaluation of the aortic root in all mutation carriers, complemented with at least 1 baseline imaging of the complete aorta and side branches.
Depending on family history and future knowledge, additional imaging of the brain vessels might be indicated.

relevance_reason: Reports a de novo TGFB3 mutation in a patient with Loeys-Dietz syndrome features and overgrowth, which is the subject of this LDS5 entry. Only the title was available.

findings.statement: Matyas et al. (2014) reported a de novo mutation in the latency-associated peptide (LAP) domain of TGFB3 in a patient with overgrowth and features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
quotes: De novo mutation of the latency-associated peptide domain of TGFB3 in a patient with overgrowth and Loeys-Dietz syndrome features.

variants.as_reported: De novo mutation of the latency-associated peptide domain of TGFB3

relevance_reason: This is the original report of Rienhoff syndrome (LDS5): one patient with a de novo TGFB3 C409Y mutation, plus functional studies.

findings.statement: Rienhoff et al. (2013) reported a 9-year-old European American girl born to nonconsanguineous healthy parents. At birth she had distal arthrogryposis, with contractures of the right hand (most severe in the 3rd and 4th fingers) and of all toes, a midline facial nevus flammeus, and mild hypotonia. She failed to thrive and had delayed gross motor development. At 17 months she had hypertelorism, prominent eyes, blue sclerae, a bifid uvula with an intact hard palate, retrognathia, mild pectus excavatum, pes planus, hyperextensible large joints, reduced muscle bulk with low tone and diminished reflexes, and markedly reduced subcutaneous fat.
quotes: The proband is a 9-year-old European-American female born to nonconsanguineous, healthy parents with two older healthy children and no previous miscarriages.
The physical exam showed contractures in the right hand, most severe in the 3rd and 4th fingers (see Fig. S1 in Supplementary online material) and all toes.
Her motor examination revealed decreased bulk in all appendicular and axial muscles, strength 1/5, low tone, and diminished reflexes throughout. Markedly reduced subcutaneous fat was noted.

findings.statement: Rienhoff et al. (2013) found that the patient walked at 24 months with a waddling gait and a positive Gowers sign, and that her neurocognitive development was normal. Radiographs showed bilateral coxa valga. She had persistent growth retardation, weighing below the 1st centile at age 7. Yearly echocardiograms from 18 months showed no cardiac defect, and her aortic root dimensions were normal (z score 0.39 at age 6.5 years). A quadriceps biopsy at age 7 showed only mild focal type 1 fiber disproportion consistent with disuse, with no dystrophic or inflammatory changes.
quotes: The patient could stand independently with a positive Gower sign at 20 months, and walked at 24 months in a “hip waddle” fashion. Her neurocognitive development was appropriate for age.
An echocardiographic examination at the age 6.5 years measured the aortic annulus and aortic root at 1.34 cm (z score 0.59) and 1.72 cm (z score 0.39), respectively

A right quadricep muscle biopsy taken at age 7 years showed normal a checkerboard pattern with Type 1 fiber predominance but mild and focal Type 1 fiber disproportion consistent with disuse or decreased usage

findings.statement: In a girl with a syndrome of distal arthrogryposis, hypotonia, bifid uvula, hypertelorism, low muscle mass and growth retardation, Rienhoff et al. (2013) used exome sequencing to identify a de novo heterozygous c.1226G>A transition in the TGFB3 gene, resulting in a cys409-to-tyr (C409Y) substitution. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the variant was de novo. It was not present in dbSNP130, the EVS database, or 1000 Genomes. Cys409 is the penultimate cysteine of the cysteine knot and is conserved across TGF-beta family ligands. No mutations were found in TGFB2, TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD3, FBN1, or FBN2.
quotes: A second de novo mutation was found in TGFB3 (c.1226G>A; pC409Y). Validation by Sanger sequencing confirmed that this mutation was de novo in the proband.
No ligand-coding sequence variants have been reported in TGFB3 including dbSNP130, EVS, or the 1000 Genomes dataset.
This penultimate cysteine is conserved in all TGFB family member ligands including orthologues in Caenorhabditis elegans and Drosophila melanogaster defining a structure called the “cysteine knot”

findings.statement: Rienhoff et al. (2013) also found a de novo heterozygous nonsense mutation in CDH2 (c.208C>T, Q70X) in the same patient. N-cadherin levels in her fibroblasts did not differ from those in controls, and Cdh2-null heterozygous mice are normal. The authors therefore concluded that the CDH2 variant was unlikely to drive the phenotype, although they could not exclude modifying effects.
quotes: A nonsense mutation was found at codon 70 in CDH2 (c.208C>T, pQ70X), encoding the 907 amino acid protein cadherin-2 or N-cadherin.
We conclude that the proband's mutation in CDH2 (c.208C>T) is unlikely to be driving the clinical phenotype, though we cannot exclude some modifying effects.

findings.statement: In functional studies, Rienhoff et al. (2013) found that secreted TGFB3 C409Y failed to activate a TGF-beta reporter in cultured cells. In Xenopus embryos, co-injecting mutant and wildtype RNA at a 1:1 ratio reduced pSMAD2 and pERK1/2 signals to about 40% and 60% of wildtype levels, respectively, consistent with a dominant-negative effect. The mutant had no effect on BMP/SMAD1 signaling. The authors concluded that the mutation is hypomorphic and that reduced TGF-beta signaling likely accounts for the phenotype.
quotes: Figure 3 shows that the wild-type (w-t) TGFB3 gene generated a transcriptional TGF-β signal, whereas the TGFB3G1226A gene construct did not.
A 1:1 ratio of mutant-to-wild-type TGFB3 RNA diminished the pSMAD2 and pERK1/2 signals to approximately 40% and 60%, respectively, of that generated by the w-t TGFB3 RNA alone.
we conclude that the TGFB3 mutation most likely accounts for the clinical findings.

findings.statement: Rienhoff et al. (2013) reported that a 3-year trial of losartan, started at age 3 at doses up to 2.0 mg/kg/day, produced no change in the patient's muscle strength or mass. They took this as further evidence that her disease mechanism differs from that of disorders with enhanced TGF-beta signaling.
quotes: At age 3 years, a 3-year trial of losartan at a dose of up to 2.0 mg/kg/day produced no change in muscle strength or mass
The proband had no change in strength or muscle mass after a significant therapeutic trial of losartan, further suggesting a pathophysiology distinct from mutations enhancing TGF-β signaling.

findings.statement: Rienhoff et al. (2013) suggested that a deficiency of TGFB3 during early myogenesis, possibly through incomplete epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition of the dermomyotome, could cause hypomyoplasia. This would clinically mimic, but be distinct from, the myopathy caused by excess TGF-beta signaling in Marfan syndrome. They concluded that normal muscle mass and complete palatal fusion require a minimum level of TGFB3 signaling.
quotes: Thus, a deficiency of TGFB3 during early myogenesis could result in hypomyoplasia throughout development that clinically mimics, but is etiologically and histologically distinct from, the myopathy caused by excess TGF-β signaling found in MFS.
we can, however, assert from these observations that the development of normal muscle mass appears to require a minimum of TGFB3 signaling, as does complete palatal fusion.

relevance_reason: The abstract covers N-cadherin's role in setting up left-right asymmetry in the chicken embryo. It does not mention Loeys-Dietz syndrome 5 (Rienhoff syndrome), TGFB3, patients or variants, so there is nothing a curator could cite in this entry.
